chapter_theme: The discus of Ayakantan wheels back to Tivittan, who hurls it and kills the king; onlookers draw lessons of impermanence, and the king's wives fall and lament over his body.

cast.role: the garlanded king whose discus turns on him, Tivittan's enemy
the young lord of Suramai who takes the returned discus and hurls it
those who see the king fall and speak their pity
Ayakantan's chief queen who faints and loses her life at the sight
the king's wives who come, fall and lament over him

1457.reading: Seeing his weapons cut down and the other's strength, the king bares his teeth in a laugh and asks whether he will still stand and fight when the discus is raised.
1457.nuance: Which weapons were cut and by whom is not named; lines 1-2 are read loosely.
1457.event: Ayakantan, taking up his discus, laughs and taunts his opponent to fight on.

1458.reading: The young lord of Suramai answers that, though weakened by the long fight, he sees the old trick of frightening him with the discus, and says the king has only tired himself.
1458.nuance: The speaker is fixed only by the vocative in line 4, which names the speaker of the reply.
1458.event: Tivittan answers Ayakantan's taunt, saying the discus will not frighten him.

1459.reading: The king twists his hand in rage and hurls the blazing discus, and the dark-hued hero vanishes inside its fire as a mountain is lost in a burning forest.
1459.event: Ayakantan hurls his discus and Tivittan is hidden by its flame.

1460.reading: The discus, spewing fire, does not strike the youth but wheels round and stands at his right side, like the sun beside a diamond mountain, while the onlookers cannot grasp what has happened.
1460.nuance: The verse does not say why the discus spares him; a reader should not add a cause the Tamil leaves out.
1460.event: The discus turns aside and halts at Tivittan's right.

1461.reading: The hero sees the discus, salutes it with joined hands, and sends it back; it splits the king's chest, strikes off his crown and enters the forehead of his elephant.
1461.event: Tivittan hurls the returned discus and it kills Ayakantan on his elephant.

1462.reading: The king, struck down, tumbles onto his elephant like a dark cloud on a mountain brow riven by a bolt of fire.
1462.event: Ayakantan falls dead over his elephant.

1463.reading: The discus sent at a man of unwavering path rebounds and kills the king who lacked restraint, as a curse spoken against a blameless man ends in the speaker's own mouth.
1463.nuance: The simile asks the reader to take the king's death as a rebounding of his own deed; it does not name a former birth, so it is not the karma of earlier lives.
1463.event: The discus kills the king who sent it.

claims.claim: a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender

1464.reading: Onlookers say that the man who came with elephants under a white umbrella and kings praising him is now cut down and brought low, and that impermanence has become plain.

claims.claim: the pomp of kings does not last

1465.reading: Yesterday he came under the long umbrella with the discus before him and kings chanting his praise; today the same man lies felled by that discus, with his golden crown still bright.
1465.nuance: The verse repeats the sense of 1464 with a day-to-day contrast of 'yesterday' and 'now'.

claims.claim: a king's glory of one day is gone the next

1466.reading: A speaker says that the discus the king threw became his own enemy and that he died at the hands of mere youths, so that even a life the heavens know seems an illusion.
1466.nuance: Line 2 calls his opponents 'boys', a mark of contempt for the king's fall rather than a statement of their age.

claims.claim: even the life the heavens know is as unreal as magic

1467.reading: Strength, killing power, wealth, beauty and splendour do not last to the end, he seems to say to those who live on earth, so do not be proud, and his fall shows it.

claims.claim: strength, wealth and beauty do not last; do not exult

1468.reading: The discus he sent at the enemy came back and split his own broad chest, and he died; who can know what will come to pass?
1468.nuance: The subject of line 1 is uncertain: it may name the king, whose body is dark, or the hero; the sense of the discus returning on its thrower is clear.
1468.event: The king's discus returns and kills him.

claims.claim: no one can know what will be

1469.reading: At such sights people pity him, and then the wives of Ayakantan, wearing gold earrings and with swelling breasts and slim waists, come near.
1469.event: The king's wives come to the body.

1470.reading: The chief queen sees her husband lying with his chest cut and her hand drops; her eyes drown in tears and life leaves her so that she is an empty body.
1470.nuance: The Tamil says her life 'left' and her body was empty, which could be a faint or a death; she is not named again in these verses.
1470.event: The chief queen faints and her life leaves her at the sight of the dead king.

1471.reading: Their garlands slip, their waists give way, and the young women fall to the ground like peacocks, beating their eyes when they see their lord's chest.
1471.event: The wives collapse on the field and beat their faces.

1472.reading: They roll about like tangled creepers flung to the earth; after a time they get up, unable to leave their beloved's side, and melt like water.
1472.event: The wives roll on the ground and rise to weep.

1473.reading: A lament addresses the king as lord of armies and of a hundred forts and asks if one who ruled the whole earth should be turned over in death.
1473.nuance: The lament reads as grief rather than doctrine: the women ask whether the fall is fitting, and the work does not answer them here.

claims.claim: a king who ruled the whole earth should not meet defeat

1474.reading: The lament asks whether it is fitting that the king whose feet were worshipped by kings and whose perfumed body smelled of musk should lie before all in the mean earth.

1475.reading: His chest, once smeared with saffron paste and a jewelled necklace, now lies bathed in a mud of blood on the elephant's forehead, which seems a thing of illusion.

claims.claim: the splendour of a king's body is like an illusion

1476.reading: Instead of the golden couch where wives rubbed his feet, he lies tipped over on a rutting elephant's forehead with the crown fallen aside; the speakers ask if that is fit sleep.
1476.nuance: The contrast of couch and battle-elephant is the lament's argument; no claim is stated.

1477.reading: The hands that the women adorned with jewels and perfumes now hang from the ear of a mountain-like elephant while vultures feed on the blood; the lament asks if that is fitting.

1478.reading: A lament says the king who gave orders like the sun and moon across the city and its halls was brought down by common men and sits bathed in blood.
1478.nuance: Several words of lines 1-3 are run together in the edition and line 1 is read loosely.

1479.reading: The women remind him that gods came to worship his discus and snakes with jewelled hoods stood by him, and ask how foes could ever have joined against him.
1479.nuance: The speakers presume the discus made him safe; the story has shown it was his own weapon that killed him.

1480.reading: The speakers ask why, with the great queen dying like a doe and other men's names being beaten on the war-drum in his own city, he does not rise in anger.
1480.nuance: The reading of 'வாழி யயனீங்க' in line 2 is uncertain.
1480.event: The wives say the conquerors are already claiming the king's city and drum.

1481.reading: The lament closes asking if he was angry with the world, and why he has left to other kings his land, his divine weapon and his wealth, when none is left to serve him.

claims.claim: a king should guard the whole world and those who serve him

links.note: In 1459 the king's discus hides the hero; in 1461 the same discus, hurled back, kills the king.
links.teaches: The weapon that seemed the king's whole safety passes to his enemy, so the first strike is shown to be only half the story.

links.note: 1460 shows the discus halting at the youth's side; 1463 explains it by saying a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender.
links.teaches: The strange halting of the discus is given a moral frame only a few verses later, so the poet explains the marvel by a rule of rebound.

links.note: 1463 ties the death to the rebound of a weapon sent against the blameless; 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy.
links.teaches: The rebound is first a simile and then a plain statement, so the onlookers read the king's death as his own act turning back.

links.note: 1462 shows the king falling from the elephant like a cloud struck by fire; 1464 turns the same fall into a moral on impermanence.
links.teaches: The poet first shows the fall and then lets onlookers draw the lesson, so the doctrine comes from the scene and not before it.

links.note: The chief queen loses her life in 1470; the other wives fall in 1471.
links.teaches: The queen's collapse leads the rest of the household, so the grief runs outward from her to all the women.

links.note: 1473 opens the laments with praise of the king's rule; 1481 closes with a question about his abandoned land and servants.
links.teaches: The women's laments move from praise of the king to a complaint that he left his duty, so grief ends in a charge against him.

links.note: 1464 shows a king who rode elephants under the umbrella brought low; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants fall when their deeds turn against them.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the cause as the king's own deeds and the verse gives the scene, so the pair joins the rule to a particular fall.

gains.a: 1464 states only that glory ends and does not name why; the quatrain supplies deeds that turn against a king as a reason.
gains.b: The quatrain states the rule in general; here a named king in a battle is the case it applies to.

links.note: 1465 says that the man who came yesterday under the umbrella is felled today; Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today.
links.teaches: The verse gives a king's fall as the proof of the couplet and adds that the end comes by his own weapon, so impermanence is shown with a cause the couplet leaves out.

gains.a: 1465 shows the fall but lacks the couplet's plain statement that loss between yesterday and today is the world's greatness.
gains.b: The couplet is an abstract rule and gains a king felled by his own discus as a case.

links.note: 1467 lists strength, wealth and beauty that do not last; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd gathering and breaking up at a dance hall.
links.teaches: The verse names what is lost, the couplet gives the image of its loss, and together they show loss as an ending without warning.

gains.a: 1467 gives a list of lost things but no image of how they go.
gains.b: The couplet gives wealth alone and gains strength and beauty with a king's body as the proof.

links.note: 1463 says a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender; Kural 319 says hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the return a rule of time, while the epic makes it happen through the victim's own hand turning the weapon back, so the return has an agent.

gains.a: 1463 lacks the couplet's plain rule that wrong done is wrong received; it only has a simile.
gains.b: The couplet gives the return without a means; the verse shows the thrown weapon as that means.

links.note: 1471 shows wives falling and beating their faces at a husband's death; Naladiyar 25 shows kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground.
links.teaches: Both pass from mourners' grief to what it shows about life, but the epic keeps the grief in the scene and the quatrain turns it into a reason to give up household life.

gains.a: 1471 lacks the quatrain's turn from grief to a judgement that household joy is empty.
gains.b: The quatrain gives wailing in general and lacks the specific grief of a king's wives.

links.note: 1476 asks whether a king who lay on a golden couch with wives rubbing his feet should now lie on an elephant's brow; Siddhar 642 says the throne of pure gold does not go with the body when Yama takes it.
links.teaches: The epic shows the couch lost by a battle and the Siddhar shows it lost by Yama, so one losing of luxury is told as a war and as the common end.

gains.a: 1476 gives a king's lost luxury but does not say that no luxury could follow him in death.
gains.b: The Siddhar verse speaks to anyone and gains a particular king's fall as a case.

links.note: 1470 shows the chief queen failing at her husband's body; Cintamani 293 shows women beating their breasts as the king lies dead.
links.teaches: In both epics the king's death is felt first by his women, so a fall in battle becomes a household loss and not only a political one.

links.note: 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy; Purananuru 227 calls Death a fool that cooked and ate its own seed by taking Valavan.
links.teaches: The epic shows the king as the agent of his death while the Sangam poet blames Death as an outside foe, so the two poems disagree on who ends a king.

gains.a: 1466 gives the fall as the king's own deed and lacks the Sangam poet's view that Death is to blame.
gains.b: The Sangam poem blames Death and gains the epic's case where the weapon of the dead man killed him.

source_issues: Verses 1459-1460 and 1473-1481 are printed in eight half-lines and were joined into four lines; verse 1460 had a stray pulli removed from line 4.
Verses 1464-1465 are short four-line verses in a different metre from those before them.
Who speaks 1466-1468 and who is named by the cloud-hued epithet in 1468 cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.
